Title: Go Field Notebook
Summary: Build a tiny typed notebook CLI while learning modules, values, slices, maps, errors and table-driven tests.
Overview:
Build a room notebook that accepts small JSON records, validates names and coordinates, and prints a stable inventory. This is your first Go program, so the deliverable includes a working module, an error contract, tests and a short explanation of value versus reference behavior.

Your existing programming experience helps with loops and conditions. Go adds explicit types, multiple return values, zero values and a compiler that rejects unused imports. Practice these on a small artifact before colony grammar makes failures harder to isolate.

Deliverable

A CLI reading one JSON array from a file argument and printing one room per line in name order, plus table-driven tests for the pure validation function. This is a notebook format, not the lem-in format. Later projects reuse the Room record and error-handling pattern.

Refresher:
A module is the build unit named by go.mod; a package groups Go source files in a directory. package main plus func main() forms an executable. A capitalized identifier is exported. A zero-valued int is 0; a nil map can be read but must be initialized before assignment.

A slice is a view over an array. Copying its header does not deep-copy its elements. Map lookup returns a second boolean so a missing key can be distinguished from a stored zero. Functions commonly return (value, error); callers must decide what to do with a non-nil error.

type Point struct { X, Y int }
p := Point{X: -3, Y: 8}
points := []Point{p}
byName := make(map[string]Point)
byName["atrium"] = points[0]
q, exists := byName["exit"]
_, _ = q, exists // remove this teaching placeholder in real code

This example introduces types; it does not validate or sort notebook records. Use gofmt to format all Go files. Compile errors are useful feedback, not runtime error cases to recover from.
Spec:
Notebook contract

  1. Accept exactly one input path. Read a JSON array of objects with Name, X, Y. Use only the standard library. Reject malformed JSON, trailing JSON data, missing names and duplicate names.
  2. Names are nonempty ASCII letters, digits or underscore; the first character cannot be L or #. For this notebook, x/y are Go ints. Negative and coincident coordinates are valid.
  3. Print accepted rooms in ascending bytewise name order as name x y, one newline per record. Do not mutate the caller's slice when obtaining sorted output.
  4. Empty arrays are valid and print nothing. Validation errors produce no inventory and return a useful error identifying the offending record.
  5. Implement ValidateRooms and Inventory as pure functions. The supplied main only delegates to Run; implement JSON decoding and output wiring yourself.

Out of scope

No tunnels, terminal commands, pathfinding, persistent database or goroutines. This small input grammar is intentionally different from the later colony parser.

Components.Title: Build the typed model
Components.Goal: Make room records and their invariants visible in types and tests.
Before: Which fields are required even when their numeric zero value is valid?
What does passing a slice copy, and what does it share?
Steps: Define two rooms with negative and zero coordinates in a table-driven test.
Implement name and duplicate validation without relying on map iteration order.
Return an error before producing output when any record is invalid.
Components.Hint: Track names in a local map, but preserve input order for identifying the first invalid record. A coordinate of zero must never be treated as missing.
Components.Trace: Trace [atrium, exit, atrium]. The third record must fail even if its coordinates differ. Trace an empty slice: no error.
Components.Gate: Tests cover a valid record, an invalid name, a duplicate, zero coordinates and empty input.

Components.Title: Build stable inventory output
Components.Goal: Separate a valid model from its presentation.
Before: Would sorting the original slice surprise a caller?
What should appear after the final record?
Steps: Create an output ordering without changing the input slice.
Compare exact bytes in a golden test and compare the input before and after the call.
Components.Hint: A copy of a slice of Room values is enough because Room contains only strings and ints. Later nested slices need a different copying argument.
Components.Trace: For input z 1 0 followed by a -2 5, predict a -2 5 then z 1 0, each ending in LF. Confirm the original first record is still z.
Components.Gate: Ten runs produce identical bytes and a mutation check passes.

Components.Title: Connect decoding, errors and tests
Components.Goal: Turn the pure functions into a small usable CLI.
Before: How can a valid JSON array followed by junk be detected?
Steps: Decode one JSON value with encoding/json and require EOF on the next decode.
Call validation before Inventory, then write the full result and check the write error.
Add subprocess or Run-level tests using strings.NewReader and bytes.Buffer.
Components.Hint: Keep file ownership in Run. main owns only process exit. Build output in memory for this deliberately small notebook so invalid input cannot print a partial inventory.
Components.Trace: Feed a valid array followed by another array. It must fail rather than silently using only the first.
Components.Gate: One valid invocation and three distinct failure paths have recorded expected and actual results.

Run:
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build -o notebook .
# Windows executable name: go build -o notebook.exe .
go run . testdata/rooms.json
Verification:
Concrete cases

The supplied JSON fixture contains z at (1,0) and a at (-2,5). After implementation, go run . testdata/rooms.json prints:

a -2 5
z 1 0
  • []: success and zero output bytes.
  • Two rooms named a: validation error and no inventory.
  • A room named Lbad or an empty name: validation error.
  • [, a missing file, and two consecutive JSON arrays: distinct error paths without panic.
  • A writer returning an error: Run propagates it.

Exit gate

Explain why map order cannot define output order, why zero coordinates are valid and why a returned error must be checked. Show gofmt-clean files and tests that verify output bytes and lack of caller mutation.
Engineering: Which invariants belong in a type and which still need runtime validation in this notebook?
How would pointer fields change your argument that copying the room slice prevents mutation?
Why can a zero-valued coordinate be valid while a zero-length name cannot?
Which validation error should win when several records are wrong, and why?
What does deterministic output buy a reviewer comparing two program runs?
How would you separate a filesystem error from a record validation error without losing context?
What evidence shows that a passing test exercises behavior instead of merely reproducing implementation steps?
Practical: Add a test with coincident coordinates and different names.
Reverse fixture record order and confirm the inventory is unchanged.
Add a trailing JSON value and verify rejection.
Run gofmt on a deliberately misindented file and inspect the diff.
Make a test writer fail after a few bytes and inspect the returned error.
Write a table-driven test with at least four name boundaries.
Extras: Add a count-only mode. Keep its output contract separate from the inventory mode so tests remain precise.
Support an optional name prefix filter. Decide whether filtering happens before or after validation and justify it.
Include line or record context in errors. Preserve the original underlying error where wrapping is useful.
Add a benchmark comparing sorting a copied slice with sorting an index slice. Measure before choosing.
Document a migration from value fields to optional coordinate pointers. Explore how missing and zero would differ without implementing a new storage system.
